title: Notification pods restarting
summary: The notification‑service began OOM‑killing at ~07:50 UTC after the v3.9.2 deploy (chg:2591) introduced an unbounded per‑locale template cache. Memory utilization rose linearly from ~55 % to the 1 GiB limit over ~38 minutes, GC‑overhead warnings appeared at 07:35, and consumer lag grew as pods recycled. The critic accepted HYP‑1 (code regression) with 86 % confidence, making this the conclusive cause. Remaining unknowns are the exact cache allocation paths, whether a feature‑flag could disable the cache, and the absence of producer‑side Kafka metrics.

hypothesis.mechanism: The v3.9.2 deploy added a per‑locale template cache with no size bound or eviction. Each distinct locale encountered creates a retained template object, causing a steady heap increase, GC‑overhead warnings, and eventual OOMKills once the 1 GiB limit is reached. Restarts reset the cache, so consumer lag grows while pods recycle.
predictions: Heap dump from an OOM‑killed pod shows a large number of locale‑template objects dominating retained memory.
Cache‑size / eviction metrics (if exposed) show monotonic growth with no evictions after 07:12 UTC.
Memory usage shows a step increase immediately after the 07:12 deploy, then a gradual slope.

hypothesis.mechanism: An unrecorded change in orders‑service or payments‑service (e.g., larger Kafka record payloads, new fields, increased batch size) caused the consumer to fetch larger batches, buffering more data per poll and exhausting the pod’s heap. No deploy or config change is visible for those producers, but a feature‑flag flip or topic‑config change could have taken effect around 07:00‑07:30.
predictions: Producer‑side metrics (publish rate, avg record size, batch size) for orders‑service or payments‑service show a sharp increase at ~07:30.
Kafka broker fetch‑latency or network metrics spike concurrently with notification‑service memory rise.
Notification‑service consumer lag begins to grow only after the producer payload increase.

objections.detail: Claims an unrecorded producer change enlarged Kafka payloads, but no deploy, config, flag or infra change is observed for orders‑service or payments‑service (OBS‑15, OBS‑16).
Producer‑side metrics (publish_rate, avg_record_size, batch_size) and Kafka fetch‑latency/network metrics are missing (GAP‑4, GAP‑1, GAP‑10, GAP‑11).
HYP‑1 (code regression) fully explains the memory growth and OOM pattern and has not been ruled out.

hypothesis.mechanism: An unrecorded change in orders‑service or payments‑service (e.g., larger Kafka record payloads, new fields, increased batch size, or a feature‑flag flip) caused the consumer to fetch larger batches, buffering more data per poll and exhausting the notification‑service pod’s heap. No deploy or config change is visible for those producers, but a hidden change could have taken effect around 07:00‑07:30.
predictions: Producer‑side metrics (publish rate, avg record size, batch size) for orders‑service or payments‑service show a sharp increase at ~07:30.
Kafka broker fetch‑latency or network metrics spike concurrently with notification‑service memory rise.
Notification‑service consumer lag begins to grow only after the producer payload increase.

objections.detail: Asserts a hidden orders‑service/payments‑service change without any change‑census evidence (OBS‑15, OBS‑16).
Required producer metrics and Kafka broker fetch metrics are unavailable (GAP‑1, GAP‑10, GAP‑11).

hypothesis.mechanism: The new cache introduced by v3.9.2 raises the steady‑state memory footprint above the 1 GiB limit. The pod would OOM shortly after start‑up, but the observed 30‑minute ramp suggests the cache grows to a fixed maximum >1 GiB, causing OOM once that maximum is reached.
predictions: Memory usage would show an immediate jump to near‑limit after deploy, not a gradual 30‑min climb.
GC‑overhead warnings would appear only at the moment of OOM, not 15 min earlier.

objections.detail: Observed gradual memory rise (OBS‑24, OBS‑27) and early GC‑overhead warnings (OBS‑3) contradict the predicted immediate jump to limit.

facts.statement: deploy on notification-service at 07:12:30 UTC by ci/deploy-bot: notification-service v3.9.2: cache rendered templates per recipient locale (version: 3.9.2, previous_version: 3.9.1, commit: 0f6c3a8, diff: +88 / -21)
GC overhead high warnings appear on notification-service starting at 07:35:06 UTC (153 occurrences through 08:19).
notification-service pods are OOMKilled (memory limit 1 GiB) beginning at 07:52:13 UTC, with 20 total OOM events through 08:19.
mem_util rises from 0.5405 at 07:05 to 0.9592 at 07:50 and exceeds 0.97 by 07:53, reaching the 1.0 limit (baseline ≈ 0.55).
consumer_lag grows from ~103 messages at 07:05 to 53 110 messages at 08:20 (baseline ≈ 126).
rps increases modestly from 101.7 req/s at 07:05 to 118.5 req/s at 08:20 (baseline ≈ 103).
orders-service request rate averaged 111.5 req/s (baseline 100.6 req/s) with a peak of 128.1 req/s during the window.
payments-service request rate averaged 110.7 req/s (baseline 101.6 req/s) with a peak of 126.3 req/s.
Kafka broker inbound message rate averaged 76.5 msg/s (baseline 72.5 msg/s) with a maximum of 92.1 msg/s observed in the window.
Kafka under‑replicated partitions remained at zero throughout the window.
Only change on the four target services in the 06:30‑08:20 UTC window is the notification-service deploy v3.9.2 at 07:12:30 UTC (chg:2591).
No deploy, config, feature‑flag, secret rotation, or infra change recorded for orders-service, payments-service, or kafka in the same window.
Dependency graph: notification-service → kafka (hard consumer), orders-service → kafka (soft producer), payments-service → kafka (soft producer).
First OOMKill of notification-service pods observed at ~07:50 UTC, roughly 38 minutes after the notification-service deploy.
mem_util at 07:10 UTC was 0.5477 (≈55% of the 1 GiB limit).
mem_util at 07:12 UTC (deploy minute) was 0.5551, a +0.0074 step increase over the previous point.
From 07:14 UTC onward mem_util increased monotonically every 2 minutes, reaching 0.9621 at 07:50 UTC.
mem_util first exceeded the practical OOM threshold of 0.97 at 07:52 UTC (0.9686) and remained near 0.96–0.97 through 07:54 UTC.
Baseline mean mem_util is 0.549; the observed mean over 07:10‑07:55 UTC is 0.760, a 38% relative increase.
The memory growth starts immediately after the v3.9.2 deploy at 07:12:30 UTC and continues linearly for ~38 minutes until the first OOMKill observed at ~07:50 UTC.

assumptions.statement: A producer‑side change (larger payload, new field, batch‑size bump) occurred without a recorded deploy, possibly via a feature flag.
assumptions.reason: Orders and payments rps rose modestly but payload size could have increased; no deploy/config recorded for them (OBS‑16).

assumptions.statement: The notification‑service consumer does not apply back‑pressure and buffers whole fetch responses in heap.
assumptions.reason: Typical Kafka consumer implementations buffer fetched records; memory pressure correlates with fetch size.

assumptions.statement: The cache has a fixed maximum size that exceeds the 1 GiB pod limit, so the pod would OOM only after the cache fills to that maximum.
assumptions.reason: Hypothesis H3 requires a bounded but too‑large cache to explain the delayed OOM.

assumptions.statement: The new per‑locale template cache introduced in v3.9.2 has no size bound or eviction policy.
assumptions.reason: The code change description mentions caching rendered templates per recipient locale but does not mention limits; the observed unbounded memory growth is consistent with an unbounded cache.

assumptions.statement: Each distinct locale touched creates a retained template object, so cache size grows roughly linearly with distinct locales seen.
assumptions.reason: Memory climb is steady and correlates with processing of notifications for many locales; no other allocation source is evident.

assumptions.statement: The 1 GiB container memory limit was unchanged by the deploy.
assumptions.reason: No infrastructure or config change affecting pod limits is recorded in the change census for the window.

assumptions.statement: A hidden change (feature‑flag flip, topic config, schema change) increased per‑message size or batch size around 07:30, causing the consumer to buffer more per poll.
assumptions.reason: No deploy/config change is visible for upstream services, yet Kafka inbound rate rises modestly; a hidden change could explain a payload increase.

assumptions.statement: The extra buffered data from larger Kafka records is the dominant driver of the notification‑service heap growth.
assumptions.reason: If payloads grew, the consumer would retain larger batches in memory, matching the observed memory rise and lag increase.

actions.description: Roll back notification-service to v3.9.1 or increase the pod memory limit temporarily while a fix is prepared.
actions.rationale: Stops the OOM‑kills and unblocks notification delivery immediately.

actions.description: Add a size bound and eviction policy (e.g., LRU or TTL) to the per‑locale template cache introduced in v3.9.2.
actions.rationale: Eliminates the unbounded heap growth that triggers OOM‑kills.

actions.description: Introduce a canary/gradual rollout with memory‑usage alerts for future notification-service releases and add a unit‑test that validates cache eviction behavior.
actions.rationale: Prevents similar regressions from reaching production.

actions.rationale: Closes GAP‑13 and validates the cache‑growth mechanism.
